comments.author: Balgair
comments.story: Why Are Plants Green? To Reduce the Noise in Photosynthesis
comments.why: Pattern in order cultures name colors.
comments.text: The perception of color is a pretty wild area of science. Colors seem to be culturally dependent. In that, people literally cannot see the difference between blue and green if their language does not have words to distinguish them. Even when big rewards are given for the 'correct' answer. Colors also follow certain patterns, with colors like blue being the last to be named in a culture. [VIDEO] Fun fact, the color blue does not appear at all in the Iliad , Homer describes the ocean as wine, despite the stunning blue colors of grecian seas.

comments.author: romaaeterna
comments.why: Linguistic explanation of color language worldwide.
comments.text: Yes, the ancient Greeks knew about the color blue, as do most old world primates. Here is an linguistic explanation of color language around the world: [VIDEO] The sculpture reconstructions you've linked are rather imaginative -- German grad students with UV lights, not chemical reconstructions -- and are probably only vaguely like the original colors. Where original colors have actually survived, in frescoes, etc., the ancients display a reasonable eye for beauty in color.

comments.author: sabizmil
comments.story: Animals are no less emotional than we are
comments.why: Example of languages defining colors differently.
comments.text: I'm not saying that emotions don't exist, just that the meaning is completely separate from the way that we define it. For example many languages define colors differently ( [VIDEO] ), but this doesn't mean that the different wavelengths don't exist. Cultures categorized them for the purpose of communication and it's only within the context of that categorization that you can understand the meaning. Earlier I referenced "finger pointing at the moon" and this is exactly it. The word is the finger and the meaning is the moon, and we shouldn't mistake the finger for the moon. > i am sure there are animals willing to discuss it with you, it’s just that you (us) can’t understand them. I was half-joking, there are already animals that we can understand and communicate with. It's just a matter of finding them :P [LINK] > it is very possible that animals feel deeper emotional connections than we do. orcas showcase some very deep emotional states. No doubt. Even visiting an animal shelter exposes some of the deep emotional state that dogs and cats can be in, and I'm sure that barely scratches the surface when considering all of the different species and circumstances.
